extracted.intended_audience: health researchers, science communicators, and health journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and measurable criteria for identifying, removing, and studying the effect of 'spin' (misrepresentation) in health news stories reporting pharmacologic studies, and metrics for measuring how news stories affect readers' interpretation. Includes classification of spin types, selection and rewriting procedures, and outcome measures for reader interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'spin'
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin is defined as a misrepresentation of study results, regardless of motive (intentionally or unintentionally), that overemphasizes the efficacy or overstates safety of the treatment as compared with that shown by the results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading reporting (example criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading reporting such as not reporting adverse events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include omission of harms and failure to report adverse events; identified as one of the most frequent types of spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading interpretation (example criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading interpretation such as claiming a causal effect despite the non-randomized study design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News stories should not assert causality when the underlying study design (e.g., non-randomized/observational) does not support causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overgeneralization / inadequate extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Overgeneralization of the results such as extrapolating a beneficial effect from an animal (pre-clinical) study to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extending findings beyond the population, species, or context studied; add explicit cautions when extrapolation is tempting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotal emphasis vs group results
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlighting a single-patient experience for the success of a new treatment instead of focusing on the group results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on anecdotes is a red flag; stories should prioritize aggregate results and contextualize individual stories rather than use them to imply general effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic spin / wording that overstates
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of language (linguistic spin) that overstates the findings; wording that increases perceived benefit or safety beyond the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors identified and deleted linguistic spin in 29 news stories when rewriting; careful wording review is required to remove subtle overstatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline-level spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin present in the headline and text; headlines often overstate or misrepresent study results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All headlines in the sample were reported with spin and were modified in de-spun versions — headline wording should be checked separately from body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of benefits and harms (absolute vs relative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should quantify benefits and harms, and avoid emphasizing relative risk reductions without absolute numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent misleading reporting included a focus on relative instead of absolute risk reduction; HealthNewsReview findings cited two-thirds of stories failed to quantify harms/benefits adequately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting study limitations and adding cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories should report study limitations and include appropriate cautions; when absent, cautions should be added according to study type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the news story did not report any limitation or caution, the researchers added caution wording per pre-specified guidance (see Table 1 and Additional file 5). Adding cautions was standardized by study type (pre-clinical, phase I/II, phase III/IV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing source(s) of spin (press release / article)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the presence of spin in the published article and its press release because spin in news stories is often related to spin in these sources; the press release is frequently the main source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A quantitative content analysis cited showed the main source of spin was the press release; checking upstream materials (press release and article) is part of evaluating the news story's accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: HealthNewsReview / journalism checklist items
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism-quality items: address cost, quantify harms and benefits, avoid reliance on anecdotes, and provide appropriate context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HealthNewsReview project graded stories and reported many as unsatisfactory; two thirds failed to adequately address cost and quantify harms/benefit. Use such toolkits to appraise reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criteria for study exemplar news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Select news stories that earned press or social media attention (high Altmetric score) and that exhibit spin in headline and text according to an existing classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers screened Altmetric Explorer results, selected 30 stories with spin (10 pre-clinical, 10 phase I/II non-RCT, 10 phase III/IV RCT), and when multiple stories existed for a citation chose the one with the most spin in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting standard to produce news stories without spin
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a 'no-spin' version: keep the same structure and content (anonymized), delete identified spin according to pre-specified guidance, and add cautions when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymize identifying information (dates, outlets, names, original article references), use hypothetical names for treatments and generic funder wording, delete linguistic spin and misleading interpretations, modify or delete investigator/patient interviews when they introduce spin, and apply a standardized guidance document (Additional file 5) with quality control checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for editorial quality control and adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use independent checks and consensus processes when identifying or removing spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One researcher identified spin and rewrote stories; a second researcher confirmed eligibility of included stories and screened 10% of excluded stories. Rewritten stories were checked by a second researcher; disagreements resolved by consensus or a third researcher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics for measuring reader interpretation (outcome measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary and secondary quantitative metrics used to assess how readers interpret news stories: primary = 'What do you think is the probability that "treatment X" would be beneficial to patients?' (NRS 0–10). Secondary = perceived size of benefit (4-point scale none/small/moderate/large), perceived safety (NRS 0–10), whether treatment should be offered short term (NRS 0–10), and whether treatment will make a difference in clinical practice (NRS 0–10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary outcome measured on numerical rating scale (0 very unlikely to 10 very likely); one secondary outcome dichotomized (moderate/large vs none/small) for analysis. These are recommended measurable endpoints to quantify interpretive impact of news stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design/sample considerations for evaluations of news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance number of reads per story, account for clustering and pairing between stories when randomizing participants to read versions with or without spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the trials each news story was read the same number of times; sample size calculation accounted for clustering (each news story assessed multiple times) and used linear mixed models with fixed and random effects and news_story × group interaction to account for within- and between-group clustering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Red flags indicating high severity spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of spin ranked by severity in prior classifications (e.g., misleading reporting, misleading interpretation, inadequate extrapolation) and identification of the most frequent/serious forms in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper references existing classifications and rankings (e.g., Yavchitz et al.) and notes frequency patterns: misleading reporting and inadequate extrapolation were widespread; misleading interpretation was especially common in phase I/II and some RCT stories.
